subject: Creativity
title: Blue Ocean Strategy: Competing by Not Competing
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Blue Ocean Strategy: Competing by Not Competing.

hook.text: Cirque du Soleil didn't compete with circuses. It eliminated animals, star performers, and three rings — then charged.

buildup.text: Red oceans are existing markets full of competition — bloody with rivals.

discovery.text: Blue ocean strategy eliminates and reduces costly industry factors while raising and creating new ones that customers.

twist.text: Nintendo's Wii competed with PS3 and Xbox not on graphics power but on fun — creating a blue ocean by targeting.

climax.text: Wii outsold PS3 and Xbox 360 despite having far inferior hardware.

punchline.text: The best way to beat the competition is to make the competition irrelevant.

quiz.question: What did Cirque du Soleil eliminate from the traditional circus model?
options: Animals, star performers, and three rings

details.summary: Blue ocean strategy creates uncontested market space rather than competing in crowded existing markets. Instead of fighting for market share in red oceans of competition, blue ocean innovators make competition irrelevant by creating entirely new categories of value.
details.whyItMatters: Blue ocean strategy provides a framework for escaping destructive competition. Cirque du Soleil, iTunes, and Nintendo Wii all succeeded by creating new markets rather than fighting for existing ones.
takeaways: Red oceans are bloody competitive markets; blue oceans are new market spaces
Blue ocean strategy creates new demand rather than fighting for existing demand
Cirque du Soleil combined theater and circus to create a new category

faq.question: How do you find a blue ocean?
faq.answer: Look for non-customers: people who should use your industry's products but do not. Understand why they stay away. Create a value proposition that addresses their unmet needs while eliminating industry features they do not care about.

faq.question: Can a blue ocean stay blue?
faq.answer: Not forever. Successful blue oceans attract competitors and eventually become red. The advantage is the head start and brand position established before competition arrives. Companies must continue seeking new blue oceans over time.
